rad.name: Curiosity rover RAD instrument (Hassler et al., Science, 2014)

lnd.name: Lunar surface dose measurement (Zhang et al., Science Advances, 2020)

storm2024.name: NASA Curiosity rover RAD and MAVEN: the solar storm of 20 May 2024 (NASA, June 2024)

moon.name: the Moon
moon.commText: A radio message reaches Earth in about 1.3 seconds.
moon.blurb: Earth answers in seconds. But there is no air, so solar storms hit HARD.
moon.why: We built here because the crater next door never sees the Sun — and its floor hides frozen water.

sun.label: Bright sunshine
sun.why: The Sun skims along the crater rim and the solar panels drink it up.

lowsun.label: Long shadows
lowsun.why: At the Moon's south pole the Sun stays very low. A mountain is starting to block it.

shadow.label: In the shadow
shadow.why: The Sun is hiding behind a mountain. The panels will charge very slowly today!

dark.label: The long dark
dark.why: A mountain on the crater rim hides the Sun all day. The panels make almost nothing, so today runs on the power cells you saved.

mars.name: Mars
mars.commText: A radio message takes between 3 and 22 minutes to reach Earth.
mars.blurb: Earth takes minutes to answer. And dust storms can hide the Sun for days.
mars.why: We built here because water ice lies just under the soil — water to drink, and oxygen to breathe.

clear.label: Clear sky
clear.why: Mars gets less than half the sunlight Earth does, but today the sky is clear.

dusty.label: Dusty sky
dusty.why: Dust floating in the air blocks some of the sunlight.

storm.label: Dust storm!
storm.why: A dust storm is hiding the Sun. In 2018 a storm like this ended the Opportunity rover's mission.

cadet.name: Cadet
cadet.blurb: A 5-day mission with extra power and longer storm warnings.

commander.name: Commander
commander.blurb: An 8-day mission. Every power cell matters, and every day is tougher.

veteran.name: Veteran
veteran.blurb: A 10-day expedition. Worn-out machines, thin supplies and four big decisions.

SHIFTS.name: Quick
SHIFTS.text: 3 minutes a day. For players who know the outpost well.

SHIFTS.name: Standard
SHIFTS.text: 5 minutes a day. Enough time for the main jobs.

SHIFTS.name: Relaxed
SHIFTS.text: 8 minutes a day. Time to explore and try everything.

SHIFTS.name: Explorer
SHIFTS.text: 12 minutes a day. No rush at all.

panel.name: Solar panel
panel.text: One more panel for the Solar Rack: about 0.7 more power cells every day.
panel.why: Solar cells are made of silicon, the most common element in Moon and Mars soil after oxygen.

battery.name: Battery bank
battery.text: The Solar Rack can hold 2 more power cells.
battery.why: Saved power is what carries a crew through a dust storm or a day without Sun.

cistern.name: Water cistern
cistern.text: The water tank holds half as much again.
cistern.why: Stored water is a reserve for dry days. A wall of water is also good shielding against radiation.

berm.name: Brick wall
berm.text: A wall of baked-soil bricks: 5% more shield for the home, and it covers no skylight.
berm.why: Engineers have baked copies of Moon soil into hard bricks using nothing but heat. No water, no cement.

rig.name: Ice drill rig
rig.text: Built on the ice field, it digs out an ice chunk all by itself every little while.
rig.why: NASA built a one-metre drill called TRIDENT to look for ice under the soil at the Moon's south pole.

turbine.name: Wind turbine
turbine.text: On dusty and stormy days it adds about 1 power cell: the wind blows when the Sun is hidden.
turbine.why: Mars air is very thin, but studies show its winds could still turn a light turbine when dust hides the Sun.

mirror.name: Sun mirror
mirror.text: A mirror on a tall mast bounces sunlight onto the panels: about 1 more power cell on shadow days, and more in the long dark.
mirror.why: At the Moon's south pole, high ground stays sunlit while low ground is dark. A mirror up high can share the light.

filter.name: Spare filter bed
filter.text: A second CO₂ filter beside the first: together they fill a third more slowly.
filter.why: The Space Station works the same way: one bed soaks up carbon dioxide while the other is baked clean.

perk.text: Useful! Crushed breccia packs tight, so the crew now fills soil bags with it: denser bags block a little more radiation.

finds.title: A piece of the first Moon crust
finds.text: This pale rock is anorthosite, part of the Moon's very first crust. Apollo 15 astronauts found one about 4 billion years old and nicknamed it the Genesis Rock.

finds.title: Smash-up rock
finds.text: This is a breccia: broken bits of rock welded together by the heat of a meteorite crash. Many of the rocks Apollo brought home are breccias.

perk.text: Useful! Moon soil is almost half oxygen, locked in minerals. These beads give theirs up more easily when heated, so the Air Maker now adds a scoop to each ice chunk: more air every time.

finds.title: Volcanic glass beads
finds.text: Tiny orange beads of glass! Apollo 17 found soil like this. The beads sprayed out of fire fountains on the Moon more than 3 billion years ago.

finds.title: Dust as sharp as glass
finds.text: Moon dust is sharp like tiny bits of broken glass, because there is no wind or water to smooth it. It scratched the Apollo astronauts' suits and visors.

perk.text: Useful! Now you know where the hard layers are, so the drill can start in softer rock: it heats up more slowly.

finds.title: Layers of crashes
finds.text: This wall shows layers of rock thrown out by older impacts. With no weather on the Moon, craters stay sharp for billions of years.

finds.title: Bootprints that last
finds.text: The bootprints you leave here could last for millions of years. There is no wind or rain on the Moon to wipe them away.

perk.text: Useful! You mapped the ice-rich layer, so every ice chunk you dig now holds more water.

finds.title: Water ice in the soil
finds.text: Ice mixed into the soil! In 2009 NASA's LCROSS mission crashed a rocket stage into a dark polar crater and found water in the cloud it kicked up.

finds.title: One of the coldest places known
finds.text: The floors of some polar craters never see the Sun. NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter measured about −240°C there.

perk.text: Useful! The old lake mud is soft, layered rock. Now you know where it is, so the drill can start there: it heats up more slowly.

finds.title: Pebbles from a stream
finds.text: Smooth, rounded pebbles stuck in rock. In 2012 the Curiosity rover found ones like these — an ancient stream bed. Water once flowed on Mars!

finds.title: Mud from a lake
finds.text: These thin layers are hardened mud, like the layers Curiosity drilled in Gale Crater, which held a lake billions of years ago.

perk.text: Useful! Hematite is a heavy iron mineral. Soil bags with it in are denser, so each one blocks a little more radiation.

finds.title: Martian "blueberries"
finds.text: Tiny grey balls! In 2004 the Opportunity rover found "blueberries" like these, made of a mineral called hematite that usually forms in water.

finds.title: Rusty dust
finds.text: Mars looks red because its dust is full of iron that has rusted — a bit like an old bike left out in the rain.

perk.text: Useful! Gypsum holds water inside its crystals: about a fifth of its weight. Warmed with the ice, it adds more water from every chunk.

finds.title: A vein left by water
finds.text: A bright white stripe in the rock. Opportunity found a vein like this in 2011: the mineral gypsum, left behind by water trickling through a crack.

finds.title: Cooled lava
finds.text: This dark rock is basalt — cooled lava. Mars has the tallest volcano in the solar system, Olympus Mons, about two and a half times as high as Mount Everest.

perk.text: Useful! This ice is very pure, with little dust or salt in it, so the Air Maker gets more oxygen out of every chunk.

finds.title: Ice under the soil
finds.text: Bright ice just under the soil! In 2008 NASA's Phoenix lander dug a small trench on Mars and found water ice like this.

finds.title: Ice that vanishes
finds.text: Phoenix watched little chunks of ice disappear over a few days. In Mars's thin air, ice turns straight into gas without melting first.

moon.name: Moonquake Sensor
moon.text: Apollo astronauts left seismometers on the Moon that felt thousands of moonquakes. They showed the Moon is still slowly shrinking as it cools.

moon.name: Laser Mirror
moon.text: Apollo crews left mirrors on the Moon. Scientists still bounce lasers off them, and found the Moon drifts 3.8 cm farther from Earth every year.

moon.name: Radiation Watcher
moon.perk: Solar storm warnings now arrive 10 seconds earlier.
moon.text: NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter carries a radiation sensor called CRaTER. Yours works on the ground and spots solar storms sooner.

mars.name: Marsquake Sensor
mars.text: NASA's InSight lander put a seismometer on Mars and felt more than 1,300 marsquakes. They revealed that Mars has a liquid metal core.

mars.name: Weather Station
mars.perk: You now get tomorrow's sunlight forecast every night.
mars.text: The Perseverance rover carries a weather station called MEDA that measures wind, temperature and dust.

mars.name: Radiation Watcher
mars.perk: Solar storm warnings now arrive 10 seconds earlier.
mars.text: The Curiosity rover carries a sensor called RAD. It was the first to measure radiation on the surface of Mars.

moon.name: Earth View
moon.text: From here Earth hangs low in the black sky. It hardly ever moves, because the Moon always keeps the same face toward Earth.

moon.name: Edge of Darkness
moon.text: The real Shackleton Crater is about 21 km wide and 4 km deep — deeper than the Grand Canyon.

mars.name: Big Sky
mars.text: On Mars the daytime sky is butterscotch-colored and the sunsets are blue — the opposite of Earth.

mars.name: Moon Spotting
mars.text: Mars has two tiny potato-shaped moons, Phobos and Deimos. Phobos races around Mars about three times a day.

DAYS.title: First steps
DAYS.learn: Astronauts cannot bring everything from Earth. They must use what is already there: sunlight for power, and ice for air and water. Engineers call this "living off the land".

DAYS.title: Shield up
DAYS.learn: Radiation is invisible energy from the Sun and from deep space. On Earth, thick air and a magnetic field protect us. Out here only mass can stop it: thick walls, or bags of soil piled on the roof.

goal.text: Put 5 soil bags on the dome today

DAYS.title: Rock detective
DAYS.learn: A rock core is a thin tube of rock pulled out with a drill. Its layers stay in order, so scientists can read what happened long ago: lava, floods, or giant crashes.

goal.text: Get 2 rock cores studied in the Lab today

DAYS.title: Calling home
DAYS.learn: Radio waves travel at the speed of light, the fastest speed there is, and it is still not instant. The farther you are from Earth, the longer every question and answer takes.

goal.text: Power the Radio Dish before midday

DAYS.title: Space farmer
DAYS.learn: Plants give a crew fresh food, fresh oxygen and a little piece of home. On the Space Station astronauts have grown lettuce, radishes and even chili peppers.

learn.mars: Dust slowly settles on solar panels and blocks the light. NASA's InSight lander lost its power this way. Clean panels mean more power cells.
learn.moon: At the Moon's south pole the Sun never climbs high. It circles low around the horizon, so solar panels must keep turning to face it.

goal.text: Look after all 3 solar panels today

DAYS.title: Science station
DAYS.learn: Instruments keep working long after astronauts go home. Scientists still bounce lasers off the mirrors that Apollo crews left on the Moon more than 50 years ago.

goal.text: Have all 3 science instruments working by tonight

DAYS.title: Road trip
DAYS.learn: A rover lets a crew carry more and explore much farther than on foot. The Apollo 17 astronauts drove their Moon buggy about 36 km.

goal.text: Bring 4 ice chunks to the machines today

DAYS.title: Pack for home
DAYS.learn: The Apollo crews brought home 382 kg of Moon rock, and scientists are still studying it today. Samples carried to Earth can be tested with machines far too big to fly.

LAUNCH_DAY.title: Launch day
LAUNCH_DAY.learn: Leaving is as hard as landing. The rocket must lift off on time to meet the ship that carries the crew back to Earth, so nothing can be left for later.

air.title: The Air Maker jammed!
air.text: A valve froze shut. No new air until it is fixed.

food.title: Greenhouse pump stuck!
food.text: The water pump stopped. Plants cannot grow until it is fixed.

lab.title: The Lab arm is stuck!
lab.text: The robot arm that loads rock cores froze. No analysis until it is fixed.

rack.title: Loose solar cable!
rack.text: A cable came loose. The Solar Rack cannot charge cells until it is fixed.

FACTS.text: A day on Mars is called a "sol". It lasts 24 hours and 39 minutes — a little longer than a day on Earth.
A real machine called MOXIE rode on the Perseverance rover and made oxygen out of Mars air: 122 grams in total. That is about what a small dog breathes in 10 hours!
The Curiosity rover's RAD sensor measured about 0.67 millisieverts of radiation every day on Mars — far more than you get on Earth.
In September 2017 a solar storm reached Mars. Curiosity's sensor saw the radiation on the ground double!
In 2018 a dust storm covered the whole planet of Mars. The solar-powered Opportunity rover could not charge and went silent after almost 15 years of exploring.
NASA's InSight lander slowly lost power as dust piled up on its solar panels. Its mission ended in 2022.
Whirlwinds called dust devils sometimes blew the dust off the Spirit and Opportunity rovers' solar panels, giving them a free power boost.
Radio waves travel at the speed of light, but Mars is so far away that a message takes 3 to 22 minutes to arrive. Astronauts there must solve many problems on their own.
Gravity on Mars is about 38% of Earth's. That is why you can jump and throw more than twice as far here.
The Perseverance rover drills rock cores and seals them in metal tubes, so a future mission can carry them back to Earth.
In 2009 the Spirit rover got stuck in soft Martian soil. Engineers on Earth tried for months to drive it free.
The Moon is about 384,000 km away. A radio message gets there in about 1.3 seconds, so Moon crews can talk with Earth almost like a phone call.
The Moon's gravity is one-sixth of Earth's. A throw that goes 6 metres on Earth flies about 36 metres here!
In 2009 NASA's LCROSS mission found water ice inside a dark crater near the Moon's south pole. Ice can be turned into drinking water and oxygen.
In sunlight the Moon's surface can reach 121°C. In darkness it drops to about −133°C. Machines need power just to stay warm.
In August 1972 a huge solar storm blasted the Moon — luckily between the Apollo 16 and Apollo 17 missions, so no astronauts were walking on it.
A sensor on the Moon's surface measured about 1.4 millisieverts of radiation every day. The Moon has no air and no magnetic shield to block it.
NASA's Artemis program is aiming for the Moon's south pole — the same kind of place as your outpost — because of its sunlight and its ice.
Loose space soil is called regolith. Engineers study piling regolith over habitats, because thick soil is a great radiation shield — and it is free!
Apollo 15, 16 and 17 each brought an electric Moon buggy. Apollo 17's crew drove theirs about 36 km in total.
Scientists sort solar flares into classes: A, B, C, M and X. Each letter is 10 times stronger than the one before. X is the strongest.

A big flare does not always mean danger. The radiation that hurts astronauts is fast protons, mostly pushed by the shock wave of a cloud of solar gas (a CME). They follow the Sun's magnetic field, so they only reach places linked to the eruption.

On 20 May 2024 a storm from the far side of the Sun, where Earth could not see it, hit Mars. NASA's Curiosity rover measured its biggest radiation surge in 12 years: like about 30 chest X-rays at once.
You cannot see or feel space radiation. Astronauts carry small sensors called dosimeters that count it for them — like your radiation badge.
Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen. The Space Station uses electricity to split water apart and give the crew oxygen to breathe.
On the International Space Station, machines recycle about 98% of the water — even sweat and pee — back into clean drinking water.
Astronauts first ate space-grown lettuce on the Space Station in 2015. The "Veggie" garden glows pink because plants love red and blue light.
NASA's Open Science Data Repository shares data from hundreds of space biology experiments — including how plants grow without normal gravity.
In low gravity, astronauts can lose 1% of their bone strength every month. They exercise about 2 hours every day to stay strong.
On Apollo 13 the air filters started to fail. The crew built a new filter holder out of plastic bags, cardboard and duct tape — and it worked.
The Space Station cleans its air with beads that trap carbon dioxide. When the beads are full, a heater bakes the gas back out so they can be used again — just like your Air Scrubber.
In 2021 astronauts grew chili peppers on the Space Station. It took 137 days, one of the longest plant experiments ever done in space. Slow crops need patience!
Every Apollo crew landed in the lunar morning and left long before sunset. Nobody has ever spent a night on the Moon: away from the poles it lasts two weeks.
Astronauts like to say that on the Space Station, yesterday's coffee becomes tomorrow's coffee. The recycled water is cleaner than most tap water on Earth.

MECHS.title: Ice just became air
MECHS.hint: Make air in the Air Maker.
MECHS.text: Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen. The Air Maker used electricity to pull them apart, and kept the oxygen. That is why it needs both ice and a power cell.

MECHS.title: Two kinds of seeds
MECHS.hint: Plant seeds in the Greenhouse.
MECHS.text: Lettuce is all leaves: ready in under a day, but a small meal. Potatoes store energy underground: almost two days, but a big meal, and less water for every bite. You choose for each bed.

MECHS.title: Plants cannot grow in the dark
MECHS.hint: Let the grow lamps run out of power.
MECHS.text: Light is the energy a plant uses to turn air and water into leaves. The grow lamps are off, so the growing has stopped. They need a power cell.

MECHS.title: The plants stopped growing
MECHS.hint: Let the water run out while plants are growing.
MECHS.text: A plant is mostly water, and it needs more to build new leaves. With the tank empty it closes its pores and waits. Bring ice to the water tank.

MECHS.title: The water tank is nearly empty
MECHS.hint: Let the water tank run low.
MECHS.text: The recycler gives back most of what the crew drinks. But growing plants keep water inside their leaves, and ice is the only new water here. Plants go thirsty first.

MECHS.title: Dinner without water
MECHS.hint: End a day with an empty water tank.
MECHS.text: Most space food is dried to save weight, and needs water to become a meal. With the tank empty, the crew had to open extra ready-made packs instead.

MECHS.title: The air filter is filling up
MECHS.hint: Let the CO₂ filter get nearly full.
MECHS.text: Every breath out adds carbon dioxide to the air indoors. The filter soaks it up like a sponge, and a sponge can only hold so much. A power cell at the Air Scrubber bakes it clean.

MECHS.title: The air has gone stale
MECHS.hint: Let the CO₂ filter fill up completely.
MECHS.text: The filter is full, so carbon dioxide is building up indoors. To keep the crew safe, the tanks are pushing out extra fresh air. That is why the air meter is falling so fast.

MECHS.title: Running uses up air
MECHS.hint: Run for a while (hold Shift on a keyboard).
MECHS.text: Hard-working muscles burn oxygen faster. In this game, running uses air one and a half times as fast, and fills the CO₂ filter sooner too. Real spacewalkers pace themselves for the same reason.

MECHS.title: The panels are making less power
MECHS.hint: Leave the solar panels alone for a while.

text.mars: Dust has settled on the glass and is blocking the sunlight, so the power cells charge more slowly. Brush the panels off to get full power back.
text.moon: The Sun has slid along the horizon and the panels no longer face it, so the power cells charge more slowly. Turn them back toward the Sun.

MECHS.title: Sunshine is going to waste
MECHS.hint: Let the Solar Rack fill right up.
MECHS.text: The rack holds only 4 power cells. While it is full, the electricity from the panels has nowhere to go. Take a cell and the charging starts again.

MECHS.title: Your first soil bag
MECHS.hint: Put a soil bag on the dome.
MECHS.text: Radiation is made of tiny, fast particles. One that hits a grain of soil stops there instead of reaching the crew. So every bag on the dome blocks a little more.

MECHS.title: The bags are covering the skylights
MECHS.hint: Pile more than 8 bags on the dome.
MECHS.text: Soil stops sunlight just as well as radiation. With the skylights covered, the lamps indoors must stay on, and that takes a little of your solar power. Nothing in space is free.

MECHS.title: Your badge is a quarter full
MECHS.hint: Fill a quarter of the radiation badge.
MECHS.text: Radiation damage adds up over a whole mission, so the badge never goes down. All you can do is fill it more slowly: more soil on the dome, and indoors whenever a storm hits.

MECHS.title: Caught outside in the storm
MECHS.hint: Be outdoors when a solar storm hits.
MECHS.text: A solar storm is a burst of fast particles from the Sun. Outdoors, only your thin suit is in their way, so the badge jumps. Indoors, the walls and soil bags stop most of them.

MECHS.title: The storm you did not feel
MECHS.hint: Sit out a solar storm indoors.
MECHS.text: You stayed indoors, so the walls and the soil on the dome took the hit for you. Mass between you and the Sun is the best protection there is.

MECHS.title: Where the warning came from
MECHS.hint: Live through a solar storm.
MECHS.text: A flare's light crosses space in minutes. The dangerous particles come after it, sped up by the shock wave of a cloud of solar gas (a CME). Forecasters on Earth watch both and warn you before most of the particles arrive. With the Radio Dish off, only your suit sensor notices, when the particles are already here.

MECHS.title: The storm scarred the solar panels
MECHS.hint: Live through a medium or big solar storm.
MECHS.text: Storm particles knock tiny flaws into solar cells, and the flaws never heal. After big storms, real satellites make a little less power for the rest of their lives. So will your panels.

MECHS.title: The drill overheated
MECHS.hint: Overheat the drill.
MECHS.text: Rubbing rock makes heat, and here there is almost no air to carry it away. Overheating wears the drill bit, and a worn bit heats faster from now on. Short bursts keep it sharp.

MECHS.title: The sample crumbled
MECHS.hint: Let the drill slip out of the green zone for too long.

text.mars: Samples break when the drill wanders out of solid rock or ice. It happened for real: in 2021 the Perseverance rover's first sample came up empty, because the rock crumbled to powder before it reached the tube.
text.moon: Lunar soil is loose and powdery, so a core can slide out of the drill if the bit wobbles. Real drill teams keep the bit straight and steady so the core stays in one piece.

MECHS.title: The rover battery ran flat
MECHS.hint: Drive the rover until its battery is empty.
MECHS.text: Running a battery all the way down damages it a little, so from now on it holds less. Real rover teams always keep some charge in reserve.

MECHS.title: Waiting for Earth
MECHS.hint: Ask Mission Control to help with a repair.

text.moon: Radio waves travel as fast as light, and the Moon is close: 1.3 seconds each way. Out here, help from Earth is almost instant.
text.mars: Radio waves travel as fast as light, but Mars is so far away that a question and its answer take many minutes. The machine stays broken while you wait.

MECHS.title: Why that throw flew so far
MECHS.hint: Land a long throw.

text.moon: The Moon pulls with one-sixth of Earth's gravity. The same throw stays in the air much longer, so it lands about six times farther away.
text.mars: Mars pulls with about 38% of Earth's gravity. The same throw stays in the air longer, so it lands more than twice as far away.

MECHS.title: Light, but just as hard to stop
MECHS.hint: Drive the rover into something.

text.moon: Here the rover weighs one-sixth of what it would on Earth, but it has exactly the same mass. So it hits a rock just as hard, and with less grip it needs much longer to stop.
text.mars: Here the rover weighs about a third of what it would on Earth, but it has exactly the same mass. So it hits a rock just as hard, and with less grip it needs longer to stop.

MECHS.title: Why the ice drill is warm
MECHS.hint: Start an ice drill.
MECHS.text: The ice here is frozen into the soil, as hard as concrete. A warm drill loosens it, and the cold outside freezes the chunk solid again the moment it comes out.

MECHS.title: More people, more of everything
MECHS.hint: Keep the outpost going until settlers arrive.
MECHS.text: Every new person breathes, drinks and eats, so they share your air plant. But more hands can also do more work. Keeping that balance decides how fast a real settlement can grow.

MECHS.title: Treasure inside plain rock
MECHS.hint: Break a rock in Pioneer mode.
MECHS.text: Moon and Mars rock is almost half oxygen, with silicon, iron and aluminium locked inside. Using what is already there, instead of shipping it from Earth, is the only way a big outpost can ever be built.

MECHS.title: Built from the ground you stand on
MECHS.hint: Build something in Pioneer mode.
MECHS.text: Launching one kilogram from Earth costs a fortune. Engineers call building with local material "in-situ resource use", and every plan for a lasting base depends on it.

MECHS.title: The long dark is coming
MECHS.hint: Stay on the Moon long enough to meet a day with no Sun.
MECHS.text: On most of the Moon, night lasts two weeks. Your crater rim almost always sees the Sun: that is why the outpost is here. But soon a mountain will hide it for a whole day. Save power cells on the rack before then.

cadet.name: Space Cadet
cadet.line: You brought the crew home. That is the hardest part!

commander.name: Outpost Commander
commander.line: You juggled power, air, food and radiation like a pro.

veteran.name: Legend of the Outpost
veteran.line: Ten days of worn-out machines and real storms. Mission Control is speechless!

air.title: The air ran out
air.text: The air tanks hit empty, so the crew climbed into the rocket and flew home early. Everyone is safe.
air.tip: Try this: plug a power cell into the Air Maker first thing, then haul ice to it. The rover carries four chunks at once.

food.title: The food ran out
food.text: The pantry is empty, so the crew packed up and flew home early. Everyone is safe.
food.tip: Try this: plants need light, water and more than a day to grow — so set up the Greenhouse on day one.

dose.title: Too much radiation
dose.text: The crew's radiation badges are full. The mission doctor called everyone home to stay healthy.
dose.tip: Try this: throw soil bags on the dome early, power the Radio Dish for longer storm warnings, and get inside when a storm is coming.
